# The Garden in Parking Space Twelve

The parking space behind our apartment building had a number painted on the wall, though nobody could remember when a car had last occupied it. Twelve. The paint had once been white. By the time I moved in, it was the color of old dishwater, and a stubborn weed had pushed through the crack beside the curb.

Every spring, someone cut the weed down. Every summer, it returned.

The space belonged, according to the building manager, to an apartment that no longer existed. Years ago, two small units had been joined into one. Their doors had changed, their mailboxes had changed, but the parking plan had not. The manager said sorting it out would require forms. He said “forms” in the tone people use for a distant and incurable disease.

One Saturday, my downstairs neighbor Imani found a tomato plant on the pavement outside the grocery store. It was in a split plastic pot with a handwritten sign: FREE. The plant was leggy and tilted toward the road, as if considering a crossing. Imani brought it home and put it in Space Twelve, where it received six hours of sun and was less likely to be kicked over than it would have been on her front step.

By Monday there were three pots. Someone added basil. Someone else added a marigold in a coffee tin. I contributed a watering can, partly because I liked the idea and partly because the tomato looked thirsty whenever I passed it.

For a while, nobody admitted responsibility. We watered whichever plants seemed dry and left the can beside the drainpipe. Then a note appeared on the wall, taped beneath the faded number:

**PLEASE WATER IN THE MORNING IF YOU CAN.**

Underneath, in different handwriting:

**PLEASE LABEL THINGS. I THINK I PICKED A PEPPER.**

The pepper was still green and small when its owner identified it. She was a woman from the third floor named Ruth. She laughed about it in the stairwell, but afterward she made wooden labels from broken clothespins and wrote every plant’s name on one. I learned more names from those labels than from the tenants’ mailboxes.

By June, Space Twelve had become crowded. The tomato produced yellow flowers. The basil grew faster than anyone could use it. Imani brought two folding chairs, and Ruth began taking her morning coffee there. People who had lived above and below one another for years discovered that they both disliked the new hallway lights, or had gone to the same school, or knew how to keep slugs off lettuce.

There were disagreements, too. Someone wanted to plant mint directly in the ground. Ruth said mint would escape and take over. A man on the first floor said the chairs made it difficult to move his bicycle. We moved the chairs. No one planted the mint in the ground.

In July, a letter arrived from the management company. The space, it said, was intended for parking and must be cleared within fourteen days. The notice was polite, firm, and addressed to no one in particular.

We held a meeting beside the tomato plant. Nine people came, plus Ruth’s grandson, who mostly wanted to know whether the pepper was ready yet. Some neighbors argued that we should move the pots before they were thrown away. Others wanted to ask for permission. Imani pointed out that permission was harder to get once the plants were gone.

So we wrote a letter. We said Space Twelve had no car assigned to it. We said the pots were movable and did not block access. We offered to keep the area tidy and remove everything if the space was ever needed. Then we signed our names. That was the surprising part: seeing how many people were willing to put their names beside something so small.

The reply took three weeks. During that time, the tomato ripened, and we harvested seven fruit, each about the size of a golf ball. Ruth cut them into slices at our second meeting so everyone could have some. They were warm from the sun and tasted better than they had any right to.

The company’s answer was not exactly yes. It was a six-month trial, subject to inspection. We read the email twice to make sure we understood it. Imani printed a copy and tucked it into a plastic sleeve behind the watering can. Within a day, someone had written **GARDEN PERMIT** across the top in green marker, although those words appeared nowhere in the actual email.

Autumn made the space less impressive. The tomato collapsed into its pot. Rain softened the labels, and the basil turned black after the first frost. Without leaves, we could see all the things we had been neglecting: a cracked paving stone, a length of loose gutter, the drain that flooded every time it rained hard.

We reported the gutter and cleared the drain ourselves. On a cold Saturday, four of us washed the empty pots and stacked them against the wall. Ruth brought a tin of biscuits. Her grandson found an earthworm under the paving stone and insisted that we stop work until it had been moved somewhere safe.

By December, Space Twelve looked almost as it had when I arrived. There were a few pots of winter greens, the folded chairs, and the weed in the crack, cut back but not gone. I had expected to feel disappointed. Instead, I noticed that I still paused there on my way inside. Often someone else did, too. We would talk for a minute about dinner, the weather, or whether the greens needed water, then carry our bags upstairs.

The six-month inspection came in January. The manager looked at the tidy pots, checked that a car could still fit, and said he saw no problem. He took a photograph for the file. Before he left, Ruth asked whether he wanted some parsley. He did.

In March, Imani started seedlings on her windowsill. She had saved seeds from the tomato. We did not know if they would grow well, and she planted more than we needed in case they did not. For a week, she brought the tray outside each morning to give the seedlings sun. By evening someone would have carried it back into the lobby, out of the cold.

The space still has its number. We never painted over it. In summer, when the pots are full, you can barely see the twelve. In winter, it is plain again, above the drainpipe and the folded chairs, marking a place that is still available if a car ever needs it.
